title: The Group Algebra and Representations of Finite Groups

items.title: The group ring $R[G]$ of finitely supported formal $R$-linear combinations of group elements
The group ring $R[G]$ is a unital $R$-algebra with basis $G$, and each $g\in G$ is a unit of $R[G]$
items.strategy: View $R[G]$ as the free $R$-module on the set $G$. Use the universal property of the free module to extend the multiplication table of $G$ uniquely to an $R$-bilinear product on basis sums. Associativity and the identity element are checked on the basis elements and then transported by bilinearity. The basis element indexed by $g^{-1}$ is the inverse of the basis element indexed by $g$.

items.title: The augmentation map $\varepsilon:R[G]\to R$ and the augmentation ideal $I_G=\ker\varepsilon$
If $G$ is finite then $\dim_k k[G]=|G|$
items.strategy: By definition, $k[G]$ is the free $k$-vector space on the set $G$. When $G$ is finite, the basis vectors indexed by the elements of $G$ form a finite basis, so the dimension is exactly the cardinality of that basis.

items.title: For a field $k$, the group algebra $k[G]$ is commutative if and only if $G$ is abelian
items.strategy: If $G$ is abelian then basis elements commute, so every pair of finite $k$-linear combinations commutes by bilinearity. Conversely, if $k[G]$ is commutative, then the basis elements attached to $g$ and $h$ commute inside $k[G]$, so their products are the basis elements attached to $gh$ and $hg$, forcing $gh=hg$ in $G$.

items.title: An $R$-linear action of $G$ on a left $R$-module, and a $G$-module over $R$
A finite-dimensional representation $\rho:G\to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ over a field, and its degree
Subrepresentations, direct sums of representations, and irreducibility
Intertwiners, the spaces $\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,W)$ and $\operatorname{End}_G(V)$, equivalent representations, and faithful representations
For a commutative ring $R$, $R$-linear $G$-actions are exactly the compatible left $R[G]$-module structures
items.strategy: From an $R$-linear action of $G$ on a left $R$-module $M$, extend the action of each basis element $g\in G$ linearly to an action of every element of $R[G]$; the resulting action satisfies $(r[e])m=rm$. Conversely, start from a left $R[G]$-module structure whose restriction along the central map $R\to R[G]$ recovers the given $R$-module structure, and then restrict to the basis elements indexed by $G$. The same formulas show that an $R$-linear map is $G$-equivariant exactly when it is an $R[G]$-module homomorphism.

items.title: Under the dictionary, subrepresentations are exactly submodules and irreducible representations are exactly simple modules
items.strategy: A linear subspace is stable under the group action exactly when it is stable under the basis elements of $k[G]$, hence under every element of $k[G]$ by linearity. Therefore the subobjects on both sides are the same, and the minimality condition defining irreducibility becomes the usual simple-module condition.

items.title: $\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,W)$ is a $k$-vector space and $\operatorname{End}_G(V)$ is a $k$-algebra
items.strategy: Inside the vector space of all linear maps, the intertwiners are exactly the maps fixed by the relation $f\rho(g)=\sigma(g)f$ for every $g\in G$, so they are closed under addition and scalar multiplication. When $V=W$, composition of two intertwiners is again an intertwiner, and the identity map is one too, so the endomorphism space inherits a $k$-algebra structure.

items.title: The trivial representation, the regular representation, and permutation representations from finite $G$-sets
The sign representation of $S_n$ and the restriction $\operatorname{Res}^G_H(V)$ of a representation to a subgroup
The regular representation is faithful
items.strategy: Let $g\ne e$ in $G$. In the regular representation, the basis vector indexed by the identity is sent to the basis vector indexed by $g$, so the action of $g$ is not the identity linear map. Hence only the identity group element acts trivially on every vector.

items.title: Every irreducible representation of a finite group is a quotient of the regular representation
items.strategy: Translate an irreducible representation into a simple $k[G]$-module. Choose any nonzero vector $v$; simplicity makes the submodule generated by $v$ equal to the whole module. The $k[G]$-linear map $k[G]\to V$ sending $a$ to $a\cdot v$ is therefore surjective, so $V$ is a quotient of the left regular module.

items.title: Every irreducible representation of a finite group has degree at most $|G|$
items.strategy: An irreducible representation is a quotient of the regular representation, so its underlying vector space has a spanning set given by the images of the basis vectors of $k[G]$. The published bound comparing a finite spanning set with an independent set then gives the degree estimate together with $\dim_k k[G]=|G|$.

items.title: A splitting field for a finite group: every irreducible representation has scalar endomorphism ring
Brauer's cyclotomic criterion for splitting fields is recorded here only as an external theorem
Schur's lemma for irreducible representations: a nonzero intertwiner is an isomorphism, and $\operatorname{End}_G(V)$ is a division ring
items.strategy: Pass to the corresponding $k[G]$-modules. The module version of Schur's lemma applies to simple modules, and the dictionary theorem translates the conclusion back into representation language.

items.title: Over a splitting field, every $G$-endomorphism of an irreducible representation is scalar
items.strategy: If $k$ is a splitting field for $G$, the definition says that every irreducible representation has endomorphism ring exactly $k$. Combined with Schur's lemma, this restates the division-ring conclusion as the scalar-operator conclusion.

items.title: Over an algebraically closed field, every endomorphism of an irreducible representation is scalar
items.strategy: Triangularize the endomorphism $T\in\operatorname{End}_G(V)$ over the algebraically closed field. One diagonal entry $\lambda$ then makes $T-\lambda I$ singular. Because $T-\lambda I$ is still a $G$-endomorphism, Schur's lemma forces it to be zero, so $T=\lambda I$.

items.title: Every irreducible representation of a finite abelian group over a splitting field is one-dimensional
items.strategy: If $G$ is abelian, each operator $\rho(g)$ commutes with every $\rho(h)$, so each $\rho(g)$ lies in $\operatorname{End}_G(V)$. Over a splitting field that endomorphism ring is just $k$, so every group element acts by a scalar. Any nonzero vector is therefore stable under the whole action and spans a nonzero subrepresentation; irreducibility forces that line to be all of $V$.

items.title: Equivalence classes of degree-one representations are exactly homomorphisms $G\to k^{\times}$; equivalently they factor through $G/G'$, and they form an abelian group
items.strategy: Choosing a basis in a one-dimensional representation identifies it with a normalized representation on $k$ and produces a homomorphism into $k^{\times}$. Two degree-one representations yield the same homomorphism exactly when they are equivalent, so equivalence classes of such representations are classified by characters. Because $k^{\times}$ is abelian, these homomorphisms factor through $G/G'$ and inherit an abelian-group structure under pointwise multiplication.

title: The Group Algebra and Representations of Finite Groups — Examples

items.title: Over $\mathbb{C}$, a cyclic group of order $n$ has exactly $n$ irreducible representations up to equivalence, represented by the characters $g\mapsto \lambda$ with $\lambda^n=1$
items.strategy: Let $G=\langle g\rangle$ with $|G|=n$. Since $G$ is abelian and $\mathbb C$ satisfies the scalar-endomorphism condition, every irreducible representation is one-dimensional and equivalent to a normalized character on $\mathbb C$. Such a character is determined by the scalar assigned to $g$, and the relation $g^n=e$ forces that scalar to be an $n$-th root of unity. The $n$ distinct roots of $x^n-1$ in $\mathbb C$ therefore give the complete list of irreducible classes.

items.title: The regular representation of $C_2$ over a field of characteristic not $2$ is the direct sum of the trivial and sign representations
items.strategy: Write the regular module on the basis $\{e,s\}$ with $s^2=e$. The vectors $e+s$ and $e-s$ are eigenvectors for the action of $s$, with eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ respectively. In characteristic not $2$ they form a basis, so the representation splits into the trivial line and the sign line.

items.title: The standard $2$-dimensional representation of $S_3$ inside the permutation representation on $\mathbb C^3$ is irreducible
items.strategy: Start from the permutation representation of $S_3$ on the basis vectors of $\mathbb C^3$. The line spanned by $(1,1,1)$ is fixed, and the coordinate-sum-zero plane is its invariant complement. To prove irreducibility of that plane, test invariance under a transposition and a $3$-cycle: any nonzero invariant line would have to be an eigenline for both matrices, and the only common possibilities are the zero space and the whole plane.

items.title: The permutation representation on the left cosets $G/H$
items.strategy: Let $G$ act by left multiplication on the finite set of left cosets $G/H$. The associated permutation representation has basis the cosets themselves, and the action matrix of any $g\in G$ just permutes that basis according to the induced action on cosets.

items.title: Any nontrivial finite group algebra has zero divisors coming from a nonidentity cyclic subgroup
items.strategy: Take a nonidentity element $g$ of finite order $n$. In $k[G]$, the two nonzero elements $e-g$ and $e+g+\cdots+g^{n-1}$ multiply to $e-g^n=0$ after the intermediate terms telescope. This exhibits concrete zero divisors inside every nontrivial finite group algebra.

items.title: The quaternion group $Q_8$ acts on $\mathbb H$ by left multiplication
items.strategy: Use the inclusion $Q_8\subseteq \mathbb H^{\times}$. Left multiplication by each quaternion in $Q_8$ is an invertible real-linear map of the $4$-dimensional real vector space $\mathbb H$, so these operators give a representation of $Q_8$ over $\mathbb R$.

items.title: The real $2$-dimensional irreducible representation of $C_3$ has endomorphism ring $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Let a generator of $C_3$ act on $\mathbb R^2$ by the companion matrix of $x^2+x+1$. Because that polynomial has no real root, the action preserves no real line, so the representation is irreducible. A real linear map commutes with the action exactly when it is a polynomial in that companion matrix, giving an endomorphism ring isomorphic to $\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+x+1)\cong\mathbb C$.

items.title: FALSE: every representation is faithful
items.strategy: Use the trivial representation. Every group element acts as the identity linear map there, so the kernel is the whole group whenever the group is nontrivial.

items.title: FALSE: if $|G|>1$, then $k[G]$ is a field
items.strategy: Choose a nonidentity element of finite order and use the explicit zero-divisor product from the cyclic subgroup calculation. A field has no zero divisors, so that identity refutes the claim immediately.

items.title: FALSE: every degree-one representation is trivial
items.strategy: On a cyclic group of order $n$, send a generator to a nontrivial complex $n$-th root of unity. This is a degree-one representation, but it is not the trivial homomorphism.

items.title: FALSE: over every field, the endomorphism ring of an irreducible representation is just the base field
items.strategy: Use the real irreducible representation of $C_3$ whose generator acts with minimal polynomial $x^2+x+1$. Its commuting endomorphisms form a copy of $\mathbb C$, which properly contains $\mathbb R$, so the scalar conclusion fails over a nonsplitting field.
